I have lived most my life in rural areas and areas with harsher than normal weather, I have never been without disaster supplies. That being said I have little for a power outage save for a hand crank radio and flashlight. I do have a battery phone charger but that will not last long in a real disaster.

I know where several flashlights in my house are. I have a camping stove & sleeping bags. After a multi-day outage a couple of years back I installed a generator - my primary aim was to power a sump pump & furnace, basically to protect the house. It has the advantage that it would also power lights & charge the phone, although I could do that with a car adapter too. I think with all that I'd be fine for a couple of days in the winter, longer in the summer. Unfortunately power outages are more likely in winter.

Invest in a solar powered battery. Some can be used to charge your phone and they are cheap and some can be used as an outlet for a while but are a little more expensive. I would suggest getting one that has a battery that you can charge from the wall and if needed recharge from solar. My parents own one and they take it camping all the time, it even came with a lamp. I'm not sure of the brand or anything like that though.

Yes. For temporary loss of electricity that's measured in hours, it's more a matter of keeping the children occupied and staying cool with no A/C or fans, than worrying about connectivity or computing. For phones we have both a travel battery and USB outlets for our vehicles. We have natural gas appliances so with some minor changes we could still cook if things went longer.

While I do admit that I am rather dependent on electricity and, to a somewhat lesser extent, gas... I think I'll be alright for a little while.

For one thing, while I won't be able to play with most of my toys, I have plenty of books to read and candles to read them by. Seriously, hundreds of votives for luminarias and tea lights for any occasion. I'm not a full on pack rat, but I do keep things that might be useful some day.

My cell eats a lot of charge, requiring plugging in nightly at the very least... but I do have a small solar array that says it can give me enough amp-hours to fully top my battery. Living in the sunny southwest as I do, emergency electricity shouldn't be a problem.

Cooking isn't bad. If electricity is off, I can always match light my burners. If gas is off, I still have my propane grill outside. Hell, that's probably a more viable option as I'll have to consider cooking whats in my fridge/freezer if it starts to defrost. But, assuming this is just a day long outage, I'm not too worried.

I suppose my biggest concern is that I wouldn't get any work done. Our battery backups there only last an hour or so with bare essentials. So, free day... but I'd be behind the rest of the week. :/

Let's look at what happens to the thermal energy that a car produces. First, the engine converts some chemical energy (fuel and air) into thermal energy, part of that energy (about 30%) is used to create mechanical energy, which is used to move the vehicle and power vehicle accessories. Some of that thermal energy (also about 30%) is dissipated into the surrounding environment by the engine cooling system, and the rest (about 40%) exits the vehicle through the exhaust. Some of the mechanical energy that the engine produces ends up lost as friction in the drivetrain of the vehicle (gears, bearings, seals, oil windage, etc), that friction converts mechanical energy into heat energy, and that heat energy is dissipated by the drivetrain components. A good deal of the mechanical energy that the engine produces is lost during deceleration, when the brakes convert mechanical energy into heat energy by using friction. Finally, most of the mechanical energy that the engine produces is lost through friction with the air and tires as the vehicle moves through the air and over whatever surface it's driving on, friction (again) produces heat.
